title: Deep Work
author: Cal Newport
tagline: Rules for focused success in a distracted world.
overview: Newport defines deep work as focused, distraction-free effort that pushes your abilities to their limit. He argues it is increasingly valuable, increasingly rare and deeply meaningful, then gives four rules for building it into your life.

chapters.title: Deep Work vs. Shallow Work
chapters.summary: Newport contrasts deep work — cognitively demanding tasks done without distraction — with shallow work: logistical tasks done while distracted, which are easy to replicate. He proposes the 'deep work hypothesis': the ability to work deeply is becoming rarer just as it becomes more valuable.
keyIdeas: Shallow work is easy to replicate.
chapters.tryThis: Label each task on today's list as deep or shallow.

quiz.question: What is shallow work?
quiz.explanation: Easy to replicate and low value.

chapters.title: Deep Work Is Valuable
chapters.summary: In the modern economy, people who can quickly master hard things and produce at an elite level thrive. Both require deep work. Newport's formula: high-quality work produced = time spent × intensity of focus.
chapters.tryThis: Pick one hard skill and plan focused sessions to learn it.

chapters.title: Deep Work Is Rare
chapters.summary: Open offices, instant messaging and social media push workplaces toward constant connectivity. Without clear metrics, people use busyness as a proxy for productivity, making shallow work the path of least resistance.
chapters.tryThis: Count how many times you check messages in one hour.

quiz.question: Why is busyness mistaken for productivity?
options: Without clear metrics, visible activity looks like value
quiz.explanation: Busyness becomes a proxy when output is unclear.

chapters.title: Deep Work Is Meaningful
chapters.summary: Newport argues deep work leads to a more meaningful life: what you focus on shapes your experience, and absorption in challenging work produces 'flow' — the state many people report as the most satisfying.
chapters.tryThis: Notice when you last felt 'in the zone' and what made it possible.

quiz.question: What state does deep work often produce?

chapters.title: Rule #1: Work Deeply
chapters.summary: Willpower is limited, so build rituals and routines. Choose a depth philosophy — monastic, bimodal, rhythmic or journalistic — then ritualise where, when and how you work, use grand gestures, collaborate wisely and execute like a business with clear lead measures and scoreboards.
chapters.tryThis: Schedule a daily deep-work block at the same time and place.

quiz.question: Which is a depth philosophy Newport describes?

chapters.title: Rule #2: Embrace Boredom
chapters.summary: If you constantly reach for your phone at the slightest boredom, your brain loses the ability to focus. Schedule breaks from focus rather than breaks from distraction, practise productive meditation and train memory to strengthen concentration.
keyIdeas: Don't flee every moment of boredom.
chapters.tryThis: Wait in a queue today without looking at your phone.

quiz.question: What does Newport suggest scheduling?
quiz.explanation: Schedule when you'll use the internet; stay offline otherwise.

chapters.title: Rule #3: Quit Social Media
chapters.summary: Rather than using tools because they offer some benefit, adopt a tool only if its benefits substantially outweigh its costs for your key goals — the 'craftsman approach'. Newport suggests a 30-day break from social media to see what you actually miss.
keyIdeas: Use the craftsman approach to tools.
chapters.tryThis: Quit one app for 30 days and note whether anyone notices.

quiz.question: What is the 'craftsman approach'?
options: Adopt tools only if benefits substantially outweigh costs
quiz.explanation: Judge tools by their impact on core goals.

chapters.title: Rule #4: Drain the Shallows
chapters.summary: Minimise shallow work: schedule every minute of your day, quantify how deep each activity is, set a shallow-work budget, finish work by a fixed time and become harder to reach with more structured email habits.
keyIdeas: Finish work at a fixed time.

quiz.question: What does Newport recommend for your workday?
quiz.explanation: Time-blocking keeps shallow work in check.

chapters.title: Conclusion
chapters.summary: Newport closes by arguing that a deep life is a good life: cultivating depth lets you produce your best work, master hard skills and find satisfaction — but it requires deliberately rejecting the distractions that dominate modern work.
keyIdeas: A deep life is a good life.
chapters.tryThis: Write one change you'll make to protect deep work.

quiz.question: What's Newport's closing message?
options: A deep life is a good life
quiz.explanation: Depth brings both results and meaning.
